title: The First Maps of the Stars
summary: How people from Babylon, Greece, China, and Persia recorded and mapped the stars, and how that work led to today's maps of billions of stars.
poll: Ancient star maps are still important today.

versions.title: Maps of the Stars
versions.text:
Long ago, there were no lamps. At night, the sky was full of stars. People looked up. They saw shapes in the stars.

A group of stars in a shape is a constellation. Each got a name. One looked like a man. One looked like a bird.

The stars helped people. They told when to plant. They showed the way at night.

So they made a map of the stars. It was in a land far away. Men pressed marks in wet clay. The clay dried hard. Each clay tablet held a list of stars. That was long, long ago.

Then a Greek man made a big list. It had lots of stars. He said which stars were bright. He said which ones were dim.

Much later, al-Sufi wrote a book of stars. He was an astronomer. He looked at the sky to learn. He drew each shape. He saw a small, dim cloud, too.

Some stars have names from Arabic. Rigel is one. It means "foot."

Now we have big telescopes. We can see a lot. Our maps show far more stars now.

Long ago, towns had no bright lights at night, so the sky was filled with stars. People looked up and saw shapes among them.

versions.title: The First Maps of the Stars
versions.text:
Long ago, there were no electric lights, so the night sky was full of stars. People all over the world looked up. They saw patterns among the stars.

A group of stars that seems to form a picture is called a constellation. People gave these patterns names. Some looked like a hunter. Others looked like a lion, a scorpion, or a fish.

The stars were more than pretty. They worked like a calendar. They told farmers when the seasons were changing and when to plant crops. They also helped travelers navigate across deserts and seas at night.

Since the stars were so useful, people began to write them down. About 3,000 years ago, sky-watchers in Babylon pressed lists of stars into clay tablets. Around 150 BCE, a Greek astronomer named Hipparchus made a catalog of about 850 stars. He sorted them by their brightness. Scientists still use this idea today.

In China, too, people drew star charts. One paper chart from about 700 CE shows more than 1,300 stars.

In 964, an astronomer from Persia named al-Sufi finished his Book of Fixed Stars. He drew each constellation two ways. One showed how it looks from the ground. The other showed how it would look on a globe. He also wrote about a faint "little cloud." Today we know it is the Andromeda Galaxy.

The Arabic names in books like his spread around the world. That is why stars such as Aldebaran, Altair, and Rigel have Arabic names today.

Later, telescopes showed many more stars. Now a space telescope called Gaia has mapped almost two billion of them.

Because the stars were so valuable, people began to record them systematically. About 3,000 years ago, Babylonian sky-watchers pressed lists of stars into clay tablets. He also described a faint "little cloud," which we now recognize as the Andromeda Galaxy.

The Arabic names recorded in such books spread throughout the world, which is why stars such as Aldebaran, Altair, and Rigel still carry Arabic names today.

versions.title: Charting the Heavens: The First Star Maps
versions.text:
Long before electric lights illuminated our cities, the night sky glittered with thousands of visible stars, and people in every part of the world gazed upward and noticed recognizable patterns among them.

A group of stars that appears to form a picture is called a constellation. Different cultures assigned these patterns their own names, so a pattern that resembled a hunter to one community might suggest a lion, a scorpion, or a fish to another.

The stars were far more than beautiful decorations. They functioned as a dependable calendar, signaling to farmers when the seasons were changing and when to plant crops, and they provided essential guidance for navigation across deserts and oceans at night.

Because the stars were so valuable, people began to record them systematically. About 3,000 years ago, Babylonian sky-watchers pressed lists of stars into clay tablets, and around 150 BCE the Greek astronomer Hipparchus compiled a catalog of approximately 850 stars, ranking them according to their apparent brightness, an early version of the magnitude scale that astronomers still use today. Approximately three centuries later, the scholar Ptolemy described 48 constellations, and most of them remain among the 88 constellations that astronomers officially recognize today.

In China, sky-watchers also produced remarkably detailed star charts. One paper chart, created around 700 CE and later discovered in a cave at Dunhuang, displays more than 1,300 stars and is considered one of the oldest complete star maps that survives anywhere.

In 964, the Persian astronomer al-Sufi completed his celebrated Book of Fixed Stars, which carefully corrected and expanded earlier Greek observations. He illustrated each constellation twice, once as it appears from the ground and once as it would look on a celestial globe, and he described a faint "little cloud" that we now recognize as the Andromeda Galaxy.

The Arabic names recorded in such books spread throughout the world, which explains why stars such as Aldebaran, Altair, and Rigel still carry Arabic names today, more than a thousand years after these manuscripts were written.

Eventually, telescopes revealed countless additional stars. Today, a space telescope called Gaia has measured the positions of almost two billion of them, producing the most detailed and comprehensive map of our galaxy ever created.

versions.title: Charting the Heavens: The First Star Maps
versions.text:
Long before electric lights illuminated our cities, the night sky glittered with thousands of visible stars, and people in every part of the world gazed upward and noticed recognizable patterns among them. Those ancient observers had no instruments except their eyes.

A group of stars that appears to form a picture is called a constellation. Different civilizations assigned these patterns their own names, so a pattern that resembled a hunter to one community might suggest a lion, a scorpion, or a fish to another.

The stars were far more than beautiful decorations. They functioned as a dependable calendar, signaling to farmers when the seasons were changing and when to plant crops, and they provided essential guidance for navigation across deserts and oceans at night.

Because the stars were so valuable, people began to record them systematically. About 3,000 years ago, Babylonian sky-watchers pressed lists of stars into clay tablets, and around 150 BCE the Greek astronomer Hipparchus compiled a catalog of approximately 850 stars, ranking them according to their apparent brightness, an early version of the magnitude scale that astronomers still use today. Approximately three centuries later, the scholar Ptolemy described 48 constellations, and most of them remain among the 88 constellations that astronomers officially recognize today.

Chinese sky-watchers also produced remarkably detailed star charts. One paper chart, created around 700 CE and subsequently discovered in a cave at Dunhuang, displays more than 1,300 stars and is considered one of the oldest complete star maps that survives anywhere.

In 964, the Persian astronomer al-Sufi completed his celebrated Book of Fixed Stars, which meticulously corrected and expanded earlier Greek observations. He illustrated each constellation twice, once as it appears from the ground and once as it would look on a celestial globe, and he described a faint "little cloud" that we now recognize as the Andromeda Galaxy, a neighboring galaxy far beyond our own.

The Arabic names recorded in such books spread throughout the world, which explains why stars such as Aldebaran, Altair, and Rigel still carry Arabic names today, more than a thousand years after these manuscripts were written.

Eventually, increasingly powerful telescopes revealed countless additional stars, and today a space telescope called Gaia has measured the positions of almost two billion of them, producing the most detailed and comprehensive map of our galaxy ever created.

questions.stem: Why might the article end with Gaia?
options: To show that Gaia replaced the need for constellations
To show that star mapping continues and has grown enormously
To explain the long history of the city of Babylon in detail
To prove that the sky has changed completely
questions.why: Ending with Gaia's nearly two billion stars connects ancient efforts to today's huge, ongoing mapping work.

wrong.A: Constellations are still recognized and named.
wrong.C: Babylon appears earlier, not at the end.
wrong.D: The article does not claim the sky changed completely.

HIGH.prompt: The article describes star mapping as work done by many cultures over thousands of years. Explain how at least two of these cultures built on or contributed to this knowledge, using evidence from the text.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
